claim: The valid split is sequential: train = days 1–120, validation = 121–150, test = 151–180.
expected result: Time order should be preserved and no future data should leak into earlier periods.
actual result: Confirmed by the project split specification in data/splits.csv and the generated data ordering.
evidence (file / cell / line): data/splits.csv; generated data ordering in data/bike_demand.csv
conclusion: This split avoids the most common time-series leakage problem.
what this does NOT establish: It does not say the model is accurate; it only ensures the evaluation is honest.

claim: Baseline A (training-set mean) is the minimum bar for validation MAE.
expected result: The validation MAE should be around 23.8.
conclusion: This is the reference baseline every later model must beat.
what this does NOT establish: It does not show that any model is better than a simpler alternative.

claim: Baseline B (previous day demand) is stronger than the training mean and is a valid naive forecast.
expected result: Validation MAE should be lower than baseline A and available at prediction time.
conclusion: This is the headline naive benchmark for the project.
what this does NOT establish: It does not prove a more complex model will generalise beyond the validation window.

claim: A linear model using only pre-day information lowers validation MAE beyond the baseline.
expected result: The candidate model should beat the best naive baseline on validation.
conclusion: This candidate is better than the naive benchmark and is still honest because it avoids same-day leakage.
what this does NOT establish: It does not guarantee that the same improvement will hold on the final untouched test split.
